title: Laser Weapons Are Finally Heading to the Battlefield: The U.S. Military Has Spent $15 Billion on R&D
dek: Lasers are called the sniper rifles of directed energy weapons, while microwaves are the electronic shotgun. The U.S. military is shifting from R&D to procurement, but the real shortage is cheap interceptors—can you win every engagement but still lose the war because you can't afford it?
why: This episode explains the real bottlenecks of laser weapons from physics and operational economics, touching on supply chains and the defense procurement landscape. It's for anyone interested in defense tech and defense stocks.
who: Defense industry analysts, defense tech VCs, readers following China's military modernization, and anyone wanting to understand the U.S. military's ammunition consumption anxiety.
skip: The first few minutes of event promos and small talk can be skipped to 05:08 where the guest's military background begins.

points.h: Lasers are sniper rifles, microwaves are shotguns
points.body: Wayne uses the analogy that lasers are sniper rifles and microwaves are electronic shotguns to distinguish the two types of directed energy weapons: lasers concentrate energy into a narrow beam, attacking one target at a time with thermal burn-through; microwaves have a wider beam that can affect the electronics of multiple targets simultaneously. The Government Accountability Office notes that high-power microwaves can reach peak power of 100 megawatts, but comparing that directly to the kilowatts of continuous-wave lasers is meaningless because their characteristics are fundamentally different: lasers aim to increase power, while microwaves aim to amplify area effects. The choice depends on the target—drone swarms are better suited to microwaves, while a single ballistic missile can only be engaged by a laser. This is because microwaves can disable drones and cause them to crash, but unlike lasers, they cannot destroy a single high-speed missile.

points.h: Chemical lasers failed due to size and logistics
points.body: After the invention of the laser in the 1960s, the military immediately saw its potential, but the real problems were power and size. In the 1990s, the U.S.-Israeli Tactical High Energy Laser and DARPA's MIRACLE chemical laser both successfully shot down rockets, but the systems were massive and logistically complex, leading to program termination in 2006. Chemical lasers derive light energy directly from chemical reactions and don't need electricity; for example, the oxygen-iodine laser was mounted on a Boeing 747 (YAL-1) to fly near ballistic missile launch areas for interception, but carrying chemicals on an aircraft was too dangerous. Today's key metric for technological progress is SWaP: size, weight, and power. In the past, lasers were as large as a building because they required enormous electrical power to generate the beam, whereas today the goal is to fit them onto trucks and warships.

points.h: Handheld laser bottleneck is power compression
points.body: When asked why sci-fi handheld laser guns don't exist yet, Wayne points to the bottleneck of power generation and compression. The fastest land-based platform currently is a high-energy laser mounted on a Stryker armored vehicle, with 50 kilowatts of power, relying on the vehicle's own generation. To get a 5-kilowatt beam to shoot down a drone, you might need 15 to 25 kilowatts of input power; without sufficient power, you can only watch the drone fly toward you helplessly. Electricity is the core constraint, not a gap in optical technology. This also explains why laser weapons have been in development for decades and are only now approaching the tipping point for large-scale deployment.

Many assume lasers can replace multi-million-dollar interceptor missiles, but Wayne warns that if an adversary launches a hypersonic weapon, you wouldn't want to gamble on a laser hitting a Mach 5 target precisely. The real framework is integrated air and missile defense—a layered combination. Lasers and microwaves have the advantage of low cost per shot, but they require the target to come within engagement range; against weapons traveling at 4,000 miles per hour, you still need carefully designed interceptors like PAC-3 and SM-3. Israel is the best example: Arrow 2/3 for long-range ballistic missiles, David's Sling for medium range, Iron Dome for rockets, and now Iron Beam for drones.

points.h: Battlefield commanders don't care about unit cost
points.body: When asked who thinks about cost when firing, Wayne breaks decisions into four levels: tactical, operational, strategic, and national. Front-line platoon and company commanders facing a threat will use whatever means necessary to protect their troops, not caring about missile costs; but at the theater command and Pentagon level, they must consider whether it's worth using a $4.1 million PAC-3 against a $30,000 drone. So the demand for cheap weapons comes from the top, not the bottom. Only national-level decision-makers incorporate ammunition consumption and supply chain issues into their choices. This distinction explains why the U.S. military, after being attrited in Yemen and the Red Sea, has begun shifting toward low-cost interception solutions.

points.h: The U.S. military is shifting to low-cost munitions
points.body: Over the past decades, the U.S. military has stockpiled increasingly expensive precision interceptors for high-end peer warfare, only to find in Yemen and the Red Sea that drones are attriting them into change. Wayne says the Pentagon is signing multi-year framework agreements to significantly increase production, but the core realization is that you can't always use expensive solutions against cheap threats. His key judgment: in future conflicts, you can win every engagement but still lose the war economically. This is the market demand for low-cost interceptors like Coyote, Vampire, and APKWS. Battlefield commanders need more options at hand, not just the ability to fire expensive missiles until they run out.

points.h: Startups are entering the mid-tier market
points.body: When asked whether laser weapons might be stifled by defense giants due to the innovator's dilemma, Wayne believes the giants will indeed continue to dominate the high-end interceptor market, but the low-end and mid-tier solutions have already gone to five companies awarded Pentagon contracts: Coaspire, Leidos, Anduril, Zone 5, and Castilian. The Pentagon wants tens of thousands of units, not an increase from 620 to 2,000. So in the short term, the giants have the advantage, but within three to five years, upstarts like Anduril could capture the mid-tier market. This also means that when investing in defense stocks, you can't just look at traditional giants; you need to see who benefits from the procurement shift.

points.h: AI killer robots are still far off
points.body: Wayne says that in the Pentagon, AI is currently used only for intelligence analysis, image labeling for analysts, and change detection—not for strike decisions. His previous research at the war college was on AI and levels of trust. Between target identification and tactical strike, it remains fully human-in-the-loop: AI can help you find targets and issue alerts, but the final decision is still made by human commanders and intelligence analysts. Some worry that AI will decide on its own to destroy targets, but Wayne says that future is a long way off. The risk models aren't ready, so the Pentagon currently doesn't use AI for autonomous killing; instead, it uses AI for military intelligence screening to replace tedious work.
